An agreement drawn up by the prophet Muhammad soon after he moved from Mecca to Yathrib, later called Medina, in the Hijra of 622. It bound the Muslims who had come from Mecca, the two main Arab tribes of the town and their Jewish allies into one community, the umma.

The document sets out mutual duties. Members were to defend the town together, pay blood money by set rules and not make separate peace with enemies. Each group kept its own religion. Disputes were to be brought to God and Muhammad, which made him the town's judge and leader. Medina's valley was declared a sanctuary.

It survives in the early biography of Muhammad by Ibn Ishaq, and most historians accept it as genuinely early, though it may join several agreements. The peace did not last: Muhammad later fell out with the three main Jewish tribes of Medina, who were expelled or killed. The charter laid the base of the first Muslim state, the root of the caliphate, and is often cited today as an early model of a shared civic order.
